meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The secret to creativity is knowing how to hide your sources'?
meta.ogDescription: No, Coco Chanel didn’t say it. The idea traces to philosopher C. E. M. Joad in 1926; the modern wording is a 1989 paraphrase first pinned on Einstein.

answer.label: Not Coco Chanel — the idea traces to C. E. M. Joad
answer.sourceLine: Coco Chanel is one of several famous names this line has been pinned on, but there is no evidence she said it. Per Quote Investigator, the earliest ancestor is a 1926 remark by philosopher C. E. M. Joad — “the height of originality is skill in concealing origins” — reworded over decades. This exact modern wording only appears in 1989, attributed to Einstein; the Chanel credit surfaced later still. So the idea is Joad’s, but the exact sentence is an anonymous 20th-century paraphrase no famous figure is documented to have spoken.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: C. E. M. Joad, The Babbitt Warren (1926)

source.excerpt: Whereas in Europe the height of originality is genius, in America the height of originality is skill in concealing origins.
trail: 1926: Philosopher C. E. M. Joad writes that in America “the height of originality is skill in concealing origins,” per Quote Investigator — the root of the saying.

1985–89: The line drifts toward “creativity is the art of concealing your sources” (Nolan Bushnell, 1985) and finally the exact modern wording, attributed to Einstein in a 1989 Usenet post — 34 years after Einstein’s death.
2012: Designer Tom Ford tells the New York Times, “Coco Chanel said that creativity is the art of concealing your sources,” adding the Chanel credit, as documented by QI.
Chanel’s own Wikiquote page does not list this line at all, consistent with an attribution she never earned.
source.excerptNote: C. E. M. Joad’s 1926 formulation — the earliest documented ancestor — as quoted in a New Republic review (9 March 1927). The familiar “secret to creativity…hide your sources” wording is a much later paraphrase.
source.rightsNote: The exact wording — “The secret to creativity is knowing how to hide your sources” — first appears in an anonymous 1989 Usenet post with no identifiable author, so no copyright status can be responsibly asserted for it. Its 1926 ancestor by C. E. M. Joad is a distinct, earlier text; this modern paraphrase is not Chanel’s and is not tied to any datable published work of hers.

author.name: C. E. M. Joad
author.heading: About C. E. M. Joad
author.bio: Cyril Edwin Mitchinson Joad (1891–1953) was an English philosopher and popular author who became a household name as a panelist on the BBC wartime radio programme The Brains Trust, famous for the catchphrase “It all depends what you mean by…” His 1926 book The Babbitt Warren, a critique of American culture, contained the observation about “skill in concealing origins” that is the earliest documented ancestor of this quotation.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook “wandering quotation”: a real idea from an obscure philosopher, reworded across decades and repeatedly re-credited to whoever sounds most quotable.

items.why: The Chanel credit appears to stem from designer Tom Ford, who told the New York Times in 2012, “Coco Chanel said that creativity is the art of concealing your sources,” per Quote Investigator. No primary source ties the line to Chanel, and it is absent from her Wikiquote page.
The exact modern wording was first attributed to Einstein in a 1989 Usenet post — 34 years after his death — and it does not appear in The Ultimate Quotable Einstein.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine origin is philosopher C. E. M. Joad’s 1926 observation that “the height of originality is skill in concealing origins,” which evolved into the familiar line, as traced by Quote Investigator.

context.heading: A quote that proves its own point
lead: The delicious irony, noted by more than one commentator, is that a maxim about hiding your sources has itself become unmoored from its source. The thought belongs to a now-obscure philosopher, C. E. M. Joad, yet it circulates under the names of the era’s most quotable celebrities — Einstein, and then Coco Chanel.
context.pull: A quote about concealing sources that successfully concealed its own.
